transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Vice President J.D. Vance says in a lengthy post
on social media that it was the unpopular war in Iran
that caused Republicans to lose spectacularly in the midterms.
Here's NPR's Emily Fang.
Vance has potential ambitions to run for president in 2028.
Though President Trump has repeatedly declined to endorse him.
Now Vance is distancing himself further
from the administration's decision
to start a war in Iran.
Writing on X, he said, quote, "Everyone
knows why we lost, and any honest conversation
about where we go from here must start there."
Vance also wrote he was, quote, "shocked"
by polling data showing widespread disapproval
against his party.
High gas prices and inflation have angered American voters,
many of whom blame the Trump administration
for a bad economy.
And on Tuesday nights, some of those voters
brought back Democratic Senator-elect Sherrod Brown
to fill Vance's vacated seat in Ohio.
Emily Fang, NPR News, the White House.
NPR's Barbara Sprunt reports Democrats in Congress
are reviewing a long to-do list when they take control
of Congress in January.
Control of Congress means control of oversight.
Democrats will act as a check on the White House, which
has not been constrained from the Republican-led Congress
thus far.
Democrats are likely to put forward bills
to tackle affordability, an issue that
propelled them to victory.
Other areas ripe for action are efforts
to reel in data centers and putting guardrails on AI.
President Trump has already said he's not
afraid to use his veto pen, but he's also
signaled some willingness to work with Democrats
and make deals.
Barbara Sprunt, NPR News, Washington.
NPR's Domenico Montanaro says Latino voters make up
a powerful bloc heading toward the 2028 presidential election.
One reason Democrats did so well in the House,
in particular in South Texas and South Florida,
was because of Latinos.
Latinos sided with Democrats 62 to 35 this time around
after swinging heavily toward Donald Trump
in the 2024 presidential election,
appeared to swing much more heavily back toward Democrats
this time around.
This really is truly a key swing group to watch.
NPR's Domenico Montanaro reporting,
one big question is whether Texas,
a state with 40 electoral votes, could actually
be in play for Democrats in a presidential election.
Democrats prevailed down the ballot
in the historically red state.
Voters ousted Republican Governor Greg Abbott
in favor of Gina Hosa, making her the first Latina woman
to be elected governor in the Lone Star state.
Democratic state representative and seminarian James Talarico
also pulled off a historic victory in his closely watched
US Senate race against state attorney general and Trump
ally Ken Paxton.
In speaking to Fox News today, Talarico
said he's more concerned with securing
economic and other relief for Texans
than exacting retribution against President Trump.
It's NPR News.
Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company, Aramco,
says its net profits are up in the last quarter
compared to the same time last year,
despite constraints on oil exports and attacks on refineries
by wars in the Gulf.
Here's NPR's Abba Trawi.
Aramco says it netted $31 billion in profits
for the third quarter of this year,
up nearly 10% from the same time last year.
That's mainly due to higher oil prices, which were up by 35%
in the third quarter compared to last year due to disruption
and supply from the US-Israel war with Iran.
In a call with investors that was live streamed,
Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said overall trade flows
through the Strait of Hormuz are a tenth of what they were
before the war, despite some oil passing through.
Aramco's oil and gas sites have been attacked this year
by Iran and Yemen's Houthis, but the company credits
overseas oil inventories and alternative export routes
for its ability to keep oil flowing to customers.
Aye-able Trawi, NPR News, Dubai.
- Former federal prosecutors now leading New York State's
investigation into the Cornell sexual assault case,
here's NPR's Alyssa Nedworney.
- The New York Attorney General has appointed Jacqueline Kelly,
a Cornell graduate who helped prosecute musician
Sean Diddy Combs to be the outside counsel
directing the investigation.
Kelly works for a private law firm and used to head
the Criminal Civil Rights Division
in the US Attorney General's office in Manhattan.
She and her team of lawyers from the AG's office
and her firm will look for evidence from the 2024 assault,
including previous investigative records,
and they'll also be tasked with gathering new details
and conducting fresh witness interviews.
Alyssa Nedworney, NPR News.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Vance blames unpopular Iran war for Republican midterm losses in social media post
Democrats plan congressional oversight, affordability bills, and AI and data center guardrails in January
Latino voters swung back to Democrats 62-35, a key 2028 swing group
Gina Hosa elected Texas governor, first Latina governor; Talarico wins Senate race over Paxton
Saudi Aramco reports Q3 profits up nearly 10% on higher oil prices despite Hormuz disruptions
New York AG appoints Jacqueline Kelly to lead investigation into 2024 Cornell sexual assault case
